Created by Dr Koh Wenjun and Dr Chew Shi Hao, NTF Anaesthesia For education only. Follow local guidelines and senior advice; check doses for each patient. Three pages Choose a region Each page covers position, equipment, sonoanatomy, needle approach, volume and concentration, coverage and an exam corner for every block. Block options
FIRST CHOICE
Thoracic paravertebral

Single shot, or better a catheter with an infusion.

Open paravertebral on the back page
→
Erector spinae plane (ESP)

Simpler and safer to place, but often not very dense. A catheter makes it last longer.

Open ESP on the back page
→
ALTERNATIVES
Serratus anterior plane

Second choice for VATS.

Open serratus anterior on the chest wall page
→
Mid-point transverse process to pleura (MTP)

An option when an ESP is unlikely to be dense enough.

Open MTP on the back page
→
Intercostal blocks by the surgeon

Commonly done under direct vision at the end of surgery, but PROSPECT doesn’t recommend them for lack of procedure-specific evidence.

Not on these pages
Practical notes
Block at a thoracic level that matches the port sites or the incision.
A catheter with a continuous infusion gives longer pain relief than a single shot.
Thoracic epidural is not recommended for VATS: paravertebral and ESP work as well with fewer side effects. It still has a place for open thoracotomy, for example when poor lung function makes the best possible analgesia important.
Thoracotomy is a bigger wound and very painful, especially a posterior incision, so plan a catheter. The 2025 MMed OSCE asked for an ESP for right thoracotomy, the other blocks you could use, and the pros of ESP over them.
Pleurodesis is the most painful VATS: plan a block plus PCA, and avoid NSAIDs, which may make the pleurodesis less effective.
If the surgeon freezes the intercostal nerves (cryoablation), it takes time to work, so you still need analgesia for the first days.
Non-intubated VATS: a block covers the skin and parietal pleura, but not the visceral pleura or the cough reflex. Add IV opioid; the surgeon can block the vagus nerve to stop coughing.
Multimodal: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, IV dexmedetomidine, and opioids as rescue.

Epidural or plane block?

Points that apply to every operation above.

An epidural is dense, covers both sides and treats visceral as well as wound pain. Plane blocks treat wound (somatic) pain only, so always add multimodal analgesia.
The cost of an epidural: hypotension from the sympathetic block, closer monitoring after surgery, and it is ruled out by abnormal clotting or sepsis, which are common in emergencies. A plane block is often still possible.
Anticoagulants: a paravertebral is a deep block, so follow the same stopping times as for an epidural. Superficial plane blocks at a site you can compress carry less bleeding risk, but still check the drugs and clotting.
Single shot or catheter: a single shot lasts hours. When the pain lasts days (rib fractures, thoracotomy, open laparotomy, open liver resection), use a catheter.
Multimodal for everyone unless contraindicated: paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, a single dose of dexamethasone where PROSPECT recommends it, and opioids as rescue.

If you choose a thoracic epidural, site it to match the incision. A high thoracic epidural spreads mostly downwards, so site it near the top of the incision; a low thoracic one spreads more upwards, so site it near the middle.

INSERTION LEVEL	USE FOR
T2–T4 (upper thoracic)
Thoracic surgery
T5–T8 (mid-thoracic)
Upper abdominal surgery
T9–T11 (low thoracic)
Lower abdominal surgery

Thoracic epidurals are not otherwise covered on these pages.

Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) has its own page, coming soon. Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks and catheters.
